newsitem.title: HONG KONG: No "privileges" for Chinese troops in HK - Patten.
newsitem.headline: No "privileges" for Chinese troops in HK - Patten.

text.p: Outgoing colonial Governor Chris Patten denied Chinese troops in Hong Kong were enjoying special treatment before the territory's handover on July 1, but defended customs officers' actions after a row at the border.

The issue has blossomed from local newspaper reports that an advance party of the People's Liberation Army Hong Kong garrison won special treatment after PLA Major-General Zhou Borong dressed down customs officers for stopping him at the border.
But Patten said Chinese troops were not being given any border-crossing privileges before China takes back the territory from Britain at midnight on June 30.

"There are no instructions to do other than apply the existing customs and immigration regulations impartially and fairly to everyone, whether they are in the PLA or whether they are in the Girl Guides," Patten told legislators during his last official question period.
A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman said the PLA advance party was "extremely disciplined and would never overstep the bounds of the law", Hong Kong government radio reported.
Patten said PLA troops had been "scrupulous" in following procedures at the border, stressing that the recent row was an isolated case.
"I think that the main reason for the incident was, candidly, a language problem -- the difficulty of a Cantonese speaker and a Mandarin speaker not communicating as well as they might," he said.
Cantonese is the Chinese dialect spoken in Hong Kong and neighbouring areas of the mainland, while Mandarin, or Putonghua, is China's official language.

On Wednesday, China's Xinhua news agency quoted a Chinese official in Hong Kong as saying a language barrier was to blame for the misunderstanding at the border and that reports of General Zhou castigating customs officers were not true.
Patten defended the actions of the border guards, saying they had "behaved totally properly".
"The way that our customs officials...handled this case was totally according to the book and they have my total support for the way they handled it," he said.

Members of the elected legislature, which is to be dissolved in 12 days and replaced by a Beijing-backed chamber, will have a chance to question government officials on the matter at a special meeting of the legislature's security panel on Friday.

A dozen protesters, angered by what they said were signs Chinese troops were above the law, handed in a petition for the PLA on Wednesday at the British forces' base in Hong Kong where Zhou and some of his 200-strong advance party are billeted.
They demanded that Chinese soldiers abide by Hong Kong law.

The presence of the PLA has prompted worries in Hong Kong, where many of the territory's 6.4 million people remember Chinese tanks and troops crushing the mainland pro-democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
The PLA has also stirred controversy with a request to move more troops across the border before midnight on June 30 so that its garrison is in place the minute Chinese rule begins.
